name: Korea Points-Based Resident Visa (F-2-7) — Complete 2026 Guide
description: Everything about Korea's F-2-7 Points-Based Resident Visa: score ≥80 out of 170, points breakdown by age, education, income, Korean language, and bonus categories, path to permanent residency, and unrestricted work authorization. The F-2-7 is Korea's premier long-term residence visa for talented professionals. Applicants accumulate points across five categories — Age (max 25 pts), Education (max 25 pts), Korean Language via TOPIK or KIIP (max 20 pts), Annual Income (max 60 pts), and Bonus Points (max 40 pts) — and must reach a combined score of 80 or higher. The visa duration ranges from 1 to 5 years depending on your total score, and holders enjoy full work freedom: change employers, start a business, or hold multiple jobs. After 3 years on F-2-7, published guidelines indicate a path to F-5 permanent residency. Updated for 2026.

eligibility.label: Hold a qualifying visa (E-1~E-7, D-5~D-9) for 3+ consecutive years
eligibility.description: Must have legally resided in Korea on an eligible visa status for at least 3 consecutive years. This requirement is waived for applicants with annual income ≥₩40M or Korean university graduates.

eligibility.label: Score ≥80 points out of 170 total
eligibility.description: Points are evaluated across five categories: Age (max 25), Education (max 25), Korean Language TOPIK/KIIP (max 20), Annual Income (max 60), and Bonus Points (max 40). Immigration officers verify each claimed point with supporting documents.

eligibility.label: Annual salary ≥₩40M allows immediate application (no 3-year wait)
eligibility.description: According to published guidelines, applicants earning ₩40,000,000 or more per year can apply immediately regardless of length of stay in Korea.

eligibility.label: Korean master's/doctoral graduate employed within 5 years of degree
eligibility.description: Graduates of Korean universities with a master's or doctoral degree who are employed or have a confirmed job offer may apply without the 3-year consecutive stay requirement, provided application is within 5 years of graduation.

eligibility.label: No criminal record or immigration violations during stay
eligibility.description: Criminal acts, immigration violations, or negligent traffic offenses may result in point deductions or disqualification from F-2-7 eligibility.

duration.initial: 1–5 years (score-dependent: 80–109 pts = 1 yr, 110–119 pts = 2 yr, 120–129 pts = 3 yr, 130+ pts = 5 yr)
duration.extension: Renewable at same or different tier based on score at renewal
duration.maxTotal: Renewable indefinitely (path to F-5 permanent residency after 3 years)

workPermission.notes: F-2-7 holders have unrestricted work authorization in Korea. This includes changing employers freely, starting a business, and holding multiple jobs simultaneously. No separate work permit is required.

faqs.question: How does the F-2-7 points calculation work?
faqs.answer: The F-2-7 uses a 170-point scoring system across five categories. Age (max 25 pts): peaks at 25–29 years old (25 pts), decreases with age. Education (max 25 pts): PhD in science/engineering scores highest (25 pts). Korean Language (max 20 pts): TOPIK Level 5–6 or KIIP Level 5 earns 20 pts. Annual Income (max 60 pts): ≥₩100M earns the maximum. Bonus Points (max 40 pts): KIIP completion, Korean university degrees, QS Top 500 graduation, community service, and government recommendations. You need a combined score of at least 80 to apply.

faqs.question: Income seems heavily weighted — how can I maximize income points?
faqs.answer: Income is the single largest category at 60 out of 170 total points. Annual income of ≥₩100M earns 60 points, ₩90–100M earns 58, ₩80–90M earns 56, and so on down to minimum wage–₩30M at 10 points. According to published guidelines, income is calculated from your National Tax Service records (근로소득증명서). Negotiate your total compensation to appear on your tax return — housing allowances and bonuses that show on your payslip count toward your reported income.

faqs.question: KIIP vs TOPIK — which is more valuable for F-2-7 points?
faqs.answer: For the Korean Language category (max 20 pts), KIIP and TOPIK score identically at each level. However, KIIP has a significant bonus advantage: completing KIIP Level 5 grants an additional 10 bonus points on top of the 20 language points, for a potential total of 30 points from Korean language alone. KIIP is also free and government-run, while TOPIK has exam fees. For F-2-7 applicants, KIIP is generally the more valuable path.

faqs.question: Is there a 75-point exception for existing F-2-7 holders?
faqs.answer: According to published guidelines, holders who obtained F-2-7 status before December 1, 2020 were allowed to renew with a minimum of 75 points instead of 80. This transitional provision had a limited validity period. Check with your local immigration office for the current renewal threshold, as policies may have been updated since.

faqs.question: What is the K-STAR visa track (32 universities)?
faqs.answer: The K-STAR (Korean Skilled Talent Attraction and Retention) track provides a streamlined pathway for graduates of 32 designated Korean universities. Published guidelines indicate that graduates from these institutions may receive additional bonus points and simplified documentation requirements. The program aims to retain foreign talent educated in Korea. Check the Korea Immigration Service website for the current list of designated universities.

faqs.question: Can my spouse and children also get work authorization through F-2-71?
faqs.answer: According to published immigration guidelines, spouses and unmarried children under 18 of F-2-7 holders can apply for F-2-71 (accompanying family) status. F-2-71 holders are permitted to engage in employment activities in Korea without a separate work permit. This is a significant advantage over other dependent visa types that restrict work authorization.

faqs.question: How does the F-2-7 lead to F-5 permanent residency?
faqs.answer: Published immigration guidelines indicate that F-2-7 holders can apply for F-5 (permanent residency) after maintaining F-2-7 status for 3 consecutive years. Additional F-5 requirements typically include a minimum income threshold, no criminal record, and basic Korean language ability. The F-2-7 is widely considered the most reliable pathway to permanent residency for non-ethnic-Korean professionals: E-7 → F-2-7 → F-5.

faqs.question: Should I negotiate my salary specifically to maximize F-2-7 points?
faqs.answer: Income documentation is based on your official tax records (원천징수영수증 or 근로소득증명서). Published guidelines use gross annual income as reported to the National Tax Service. If your employer provides separate housing allowances, meal stipends, or other non-taxable benefits, these may not appear on your income certificate. Consider negotiating a higher base salary that includes these benefits, so your tax records reflect a higher total income.

faqs.question: Do volunteering hours and blood donation count toward bonus points?
faqs.answer: According to published guidelines, domestic community service activities can earn 1–7 bonus points depending on duration: 1 year of activity earns 1 point, 2 years earns 3 points, and 3+ years earns 7 points. Blood donation at Korean Red Cross facilities is recognized as community service hours. You need documentation (봉사활동 확인서) from 1365 Volunteer Portal or the organization where you volunteered.

faqs.question: Is the Korean language requirement mandatory for F-2-7?
faqs.answer: Korean language proficiency (TOPIK/KIIP) is not a mandatory requirement for F-2-7 — it is one of five scoring categories contributing up to 20 points. You can reach 80 points without any Korean language score if you accumulate sufficient points from income, education, age, and bonus categories. However, KIIP Level 5 completion adds a valuable 10 bonus points. For applicants with high income (≥₩50M) and a relevant degree, the language category may not be necessary to reach the threshold.

faqs.question: Can I apply for F-2-7 from outside Korea?
faqs.answer: No. According to published immigration procedures, F-2-7 is a change-of-status visa that must be applied for in person at a Korean immigration office (출입국·외국인청). You must already be residing in Korea on a qualifying visa (E-1–E-7, D-5–D-9) when you apply. The application cannot be submitted at Korean embassies or consulates abroad.

faqs.question: What happens if my score drops below 80 at renewal?
faqs.answer: At each renewal, immigration officers re-evaluate your total score based on current circumstances. If your score falls below 80 — for example, due to aging out of a higher age bracket, job loss, or income decrease — published guidelines indicate your F-2-7 renewal may be denied. You would need to revert to your previous visa type or find another qualifying status. Plan ahead: track your projected score at renewal time, and consider increasing points in categories you can control (income, language, community service).

communityTips.tip: Income scores make up 60 out of 170 total points. If your annual salary exceeds ₩40M, published guidelines indicate you can apply immediately without the 3-year stay requirement. Focus on getting your salary as high as possible on paper.

Instead of accepting a split like '2.5M salary + 0.5M housing allowance,' negotiate a flat 3M salary. Your tax return reflects higher income, which translates directly to more F-2-7 points. The income certificate from Hometax only shows taxable income.

KIIP (사회통합프로그램) Level 5 completion gives you 10 extra bonus points on top of the 20 language points — a total of 30 points from Korean language alone. It is free, government-run, and the most point-efficient investment of your time.

Blood donation at Korean Red Cross counts as community service hours toward the volunteering bonus points. You need documented activity over multiple occasions to build up credit. Register your volunteer hours on the 1365 portal.

Start preparing 2–3 years before you need the F-2-7. TOPIK study, KIIP enrollment, salary negotiations, and community service hours all take time. Many professionals realize too late that they are short on points and cannot catch up quickly.

pathsFrom.name: Professional Employment Visa
pathsFrom.requirements: Hold E-7 status for 3+ consecutive years, OR have annual salary ≥₩40M (apply immediately). Score ≥80 points on the F-2-7 points system.
pathsFrom.notes: The most common transition path. E-7 holders with strong income and education credentials often accumulate 80+ points within their first few years. The E-7 → F-2-7 → F-5 pathway is the standard route to permanent residency.

pathsFrom.name: Corporate Investment Visa
pathsFrom.requirements: Hold D-8 status and meet the ≥80 point threshold. Business income reported to NTS counts toward income points.
documents: Income tax records from business operations
pathsFrom.notes: D-8 holders with successful businesses generating strong income can transition to F-2-7 for more flexible residency rights. Business income must be verifiable through NTS records.

pathsFrom.name: Teaching (Foreign Language Instructor) Visa
pathsFrom.requirements: Hold E-2 status for 3+ consecutive years and score ≥80 points. E-2 salaries are typically lower, so strong education and language scores are important.
pathsFrom.notes: E-2 holders face a challenge because teaching salaries are often in the ₩25–35M range, yielding only 10–30 income points. Maximizing education, language, and bonus points is critical for E-2 to F-2-7 transitions.

pathsFrom.name: Student Visa
pathsFrom.requirements: Graduate from a Korean university, then transition through D-10 (job seeking) and E-series (employment) visas. After 3+ years on E-series or meeting income requirements, apply for F-2-7.
pathsFrom.timeline: Multi-year pathway: D-2 → D-10 → E-7 → F-2-7
pathsFrom.notes: Korean university graduates receive bonus points (Bachelor's +5, Master's/PhD +10) which significantly helps reach the 80-point threshold. Combined D-2 and D-10 time may count toward the 3-year residency requirement according to published guidelines.
